speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, related to these conferences may I ask the Prime Minister if he will comment on the accuracy of press reports to the effect that during the United Kingdom Prime Minister's visit our Prime


Minister intervened to prevent a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation commentator from asking Prime Minister Macmillan a question about the United Kingdom free trade offer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to do that. As a matter of fact what actually took place was this. Following a press conference at which matters were very fully discussed there was a meeting between the Prime Minister and myself. We discussed various matters, it being understood that thereafter there would be a joint conference before the C.B.C. When we came out we met with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation representatives and just before the interview commenced the Prime Minister asked what the questions were. As I recall it the first question on the list of two was as to whether or not the representations or the so-called proposal advanced last September regarding free trade with the United Kingdom would be on the agenda of the trade conference this fall. I said, "No, no," and then that terminated it as far as I was concerned. Naturally, thereafter I was surprised to find the comment that was made respecting what took place. In point of fact a mountain was made out of a molehill.
I can only say in so far as this government is concerned at no time has there ever been, directly or indirectly, any interference with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; and the nature of the observations made from time to time by commentators regarding this government and its undertakings since it came into power would be an effective answer to anyone who would suggest the contrary. In other words, there has not been and will not be any interference of this kind on the part of this government, either directly or indirectly, and there was no suggestion of that in any way the other day nor will there be at any other time. After all, while we may disagree with what is said about us, and while criticism of those in public life is sometimes not factual, the essence of democracy is the preservation of the right to make such criticism.
In so far as this question is concerned, I can only say that there was nothing whatsoever to justify the conclusions that were arrived at in various quarters. There is nothing to conceal about the offer. Questions concerning this matter had been fully asked at the press conference, and my information is that last evening full and complete discussions took place by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom regarding this offer or proposal, so-called.
No attempt in any way was made to interfere nor will there ever be, which is something

different from what happened when the last government was in power.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, arising out of the Prime Minister's answer, am I to understand that the statement attributed to him, not by one but by a number of reputable newspaper correspondents, "No, no, you cannot ask that question", then had nothing whatever to do with the question that Mr. Macmillan might have been asked by the C.B.C. reporter regarding free trade?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I have nothing really to
add to what I have already said. Any question that arose was in consequence of his request as to the nature of the questions that were to be asked. In other words, he wanted to know in advance. As far as any other matter is concerned, I can only say this: that there is no ground for any lamentation over this as being an invasion in any way of the right of the C.B.C. to express its views, or of anyone to express his or her views regardless of whether it is critical of the government or not, as is apparent to every person in this country since this government came into power.

TOLLS CHARGED ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY
speechtext: I thought at this particular time I should like to bring up a matter that is vital to the economy of Canada, namely the proposed tolls on the St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland ship canal. Not since the early 1900's has any toll been charged on any canals or locks from lake Erie to the sea-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TOLLS CHARGED ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but may I ask the members if they will kindly settle themselves and moderate their conversations so the hon. member can be heard.

maintopic: TOLLS CHARGED ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY
speechtext:
I was going on, Mr. Speaker, to say that not since early in the 1900's have any tolls been charged on any canals or locks between lake Erie and the sea.
According to the statement which the Minister of Transport made in this house not long ago, the proposed tolls are to be announced around July 1 and at that time shipping and other interests would have an opportunity to make representations in connection therewith. According to reports emanating from Washington, and more recently from Ottawa, it is estimated that the average tonnage passing through the St. Lawrence seaway over the first four or five years will be in the neighbourhood of 41.5 million tons each year; and Mr. Reese Harill, the chairman of the United States tolls committee, has made a statement as follows:
We will not be too far oft from the target of $1.25 per ton for general cargo and 50 cents per ton for bulk.
I have also seen statements from Washington indicating that observers in that city

St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls believed that the toll charges would be greater than these amounts and I was wondering if the Canadian members of the toll committee thought they could go along with the toll of $1.25 and 50 cents, in view of this feeling in Washington. I would like to know from the minister if the Canadian members were insisting on these last mentioned rates.
The locks on the Welland canal conform in size with those presently being constructed on the St. Lawrence seaway, and the only work being done on the Welland canal is the deepening of the sailing levels at a cost of something under $30 million. As members of parliament we should be interested in the costs of vessel operation in so far as they relate to the cost of moving cargo. We should consider what effect this cost may have on industry generally, on agriculture and commerce. We should be interested in the shipping industry because of the thousands of men who are engaged as seamen and because of the shipbuilders and suppliers, in the same way that we should be interested in the welfare of Canada generally.
I have often read that 40 per cent of our workmen depend for their livelihood upon our foreign trade, and I believe that if we are to have a continuing prosperity in this country we must have an expanding trade. The St. Lawrence river and the great lakes basin, which extends to the very heart of our continent, a distance of 2,900 miles from the sea, are Canada's greatest single outlet to the markets of Europe, the western coast of the United States and South America. Much of the trade between Canada and the United States goes across this route. The water transportation in this area is called the most economical transportation system in the world and, because of its economy, it has helped to build up our country. It has helped our farmers to market their wheat in highly competitive markets, even though that wheat is grown thousands of miles from the seaports. It has also helped our industry to assemble raw materials, to manufacture products and to enter competitive markets. Today this water transportation system is becoming even more important to the economy of Canada because of the prospective shipping of large tonnages of iron ore from Quebec and Labrador to steel centres along the great lakes in both Canada and the United States.
I read over the bill authorizing the setting up of the St. Lawrence seaway authority to charge tolls. Those tolls charges are to cover the operation of the canals plus the amortization charges, which are to be retired in 50 years. The bill received the support of


all parties in this house when it was passed in 1951. There was no division on any reading of the bill, and the only opposition I could find in reading over the debates was that this St. Lawrence seaway was being built as window dressing for the Ontario hydro-electric power commission, which at that time particularly needed power.
In order to meet United States legislative requirements the tolls must pay off the United States' contribution of $140 million which, because of higher cost of construction, is today around $165 million. We must pay this amount off in 50 years as well as operate the canal itself. If the same applies to the Canadian contribution, something in the nature of $30 million per year will be required to be raised by means of tolls. It will be well, therefore, to examine the volume of trade now making use of the canals and the increased tonnages of iron ore likely to move up through those canals from Quebec and Labrador to the Canadian and United States steel centres.
First of all, in the year 1956, which is the last year for which figures are available, traffic through the Welland canal amounted to 23.1 million tons and that through the St. Lawrence canals to 13.5 million tons. In that year Canadian coastal shipping accounted for one-third of the traffic through the Welland canal and one-half of the traffic through the St. Lawrence canals, while United States coastal shipping accounted for only 6 per cent of the traffic through the Welland canal and less than one-half of one per cent of the traffic through the St. Lawrence canals. Most of the international trade is made up of imports of soft coal to lake Ontario ports and to Montreal, petroleum and other oils and paper, and last year 2.8 million tons of iron ore from Seven Islands were shipped to the United States steel industry.
Direct overseas shipping is increasing, but last year it accounted for only about 6 per cent of the tonnage going through the St. Lawrence river. It is difficult to arrive at a figure, but it would seem that Canada makes use of about 90 per cent of these lower canals and that the United States makes use of something less than 10 per cent. It is therefore only reasonable that tolls should be set to encourage United States shipping and to at least ensure that our tonnages of iron ore will pass through these lower canals-that is to say, the St. Lawrence and Welland canals-to help us pay for the cost of operating them plus the amortization charges.
I said earlier that the Welland canal was being deepened at a cost of something under $30 million and that the tonnages going through amounted to 23.1 million tons in

1956. It is therefore easy to see that the cost of the current deepening of that canal could be retired over a period of 50 years by a charge of just a few cents per ton. It would appear to me to be unreasonable and unfair to charge the Welland canal with more than this $30 million figure because you would then, for example, be charging the importers in Toronto or in Hamilton-and they make a great deal of use of the canal-tolls in excess of what they should pay.
If this were done it would be asking them to pay some of the cost of the St. Lawrence seaway although they would not be making any use of the seaway. After all, tonnage moving through the Welland canal is about twice that moving through the lower canal, the St. Lawrence seaway. For this reason I have always thought it wrong to include the Welland canal as part of the St. Lawrence seaway, because nearly half the tonnage through the Welland canal never reaches the St. Lawrence river.
There are certain basic concepts which our government should keep in mind before reaching an agreement with the United States on the amount of tolls to be charged. First, it should be remembered that lake Ontario and the Welland canal are the sites of the major part of Ontario industry making use of water shipping. Lake Ontario will be the only lake of all the great lakes that will be toll-locked, requiring tolls at both ends before ships are allowed either to enter or leave.
The shores of lake Ontario are the source of little raw material for industry. Therefore most of our Ontario industry bringing in raw material by boat for processing will have to pay a toll charge on it, no matter what the source. This is not true of most of the competitive American plants. The Steel Company of Canada Limited at Hamilton, for example, would be required to bring in three and a half tons of raw material through a toll area to make one ton of steel, while steel companies at Buffalo and Cleveland would have no tolls to pay on any of their raw materials.
Second, it should also be borne in mind that the St. Lawrence seaway is not such a major factor in the economy of the United States. If the tolls on the seaway are too high the United States has alternative water and other routes to carry its heavy commerce, while Canada, because of its geography has not.
Certainly the United States makes comparatively little use of the canals at the present time. In the Chicago area and the American mid-west much of their commerce goes down the Mississippi, while the eastern railways in the United States can deliver Quebec and Labrador ore to such American steel 57071-3-74
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls centres in central and southern Ohio from 'special docks at Baltimore cheaper than by ship through the St. Lawrence seaway even at the present time. If we are not successful in collecting tolls on a very large part of our own iron ore from Labrador and Quebec destined for American mills, then the toll charges on our own shipping will be increased. If we had double the shipping we would have half the toll charge.
The eastern railways always opposed the St. Lawrence seaway construction, and it is only natural for them to lobby to get the tolls as high as possible to increase their own business in the movement of this ore. The United States government spent $150 million for construction of a canal at Baltimore. I understand that six ships having a capacity of 40,000 to 60,000 tons each are now being constructed to carry this Canadian ore to Baltimore, while only two new 25,000 ton ships are being made ready to transport ore through the seaway, and I also know that some canal boats now operating through the Welland canal will be able to operate through the St. Lawrence canal and carry this iron ore.
The higher the tolls the more the United States shipping and our own ore will be diverted to other routes, and the more our Canadian shipping will be left holding the bag. I saw a statement not long ago, originating in Washington, which suggested there should be a maximum charge over the first four or five years to pay all charges, after which these charges might be lowered as the tonnage increased. I hope that such a high toll will not be set in the early years of transition from small canallers to large carriers, because it will take a few years to replace the smaller boats, and consequently shipping charges per ton in the earlier period of use will remain high. Mr. Harrill, chairman of the United States toll committee, said the job of the joint committee is to reconcile the United States legislative necessity of paying off the cost of the seaway in 50 years with having tolls low enough to attract traffic.
Surely this statement allows our members on the joint committee to bargain for low toll charges until maximum tonnages have been established. The United States government did the deepening and the building of two locks in the international part of the St. Lawrence river. This comprises rather a small share of the total cost of St. Lawrence seaway project, the rest of it being in the province of Quebec, and the Welland canal lying wholly within Canadian territory in the Niagara district.
I do not like the lever that the smaller expenditure of $140 million seems to give the

St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls United States over the tolls, because almost every dispatch from Washington seems to emphasize their legislative monetary requirements for the next 50 years. There are reports of many pressure groups in the United States wanting the tolls as high as possible in order to gain tonnages for their own transport systems.
I agree that there should be a joint tolls committee to deal with the international part of the seaway, and to correlate it with the other major part which is wholly within Canada. However, I cannot help but resent a foreign power being given any direction or say over the operation of any canals within our own country. To me it is akin to surrendering some part of our sovereignty by giving them some direct voice in our economy for the next 50-years; and this over the years, could lead to ill-will and distrust among the peoples of two friendly nations.
Hon. members will all recall the difficulty in getting the seaway and power project underway. The Ontario government was badly in need of more power; and while public opinion in Canada would have supported Canada doing the whole project alone, it could not be done without the acquiescence of the United States as it involved flooding some of that country's sovereign land. The principle of tolls was accepted, but our government reserved the right to build her own two locks at Cornwall and then have an all-Canadian waterway.
It is interesting to note that the shipping tonnage through Sault Ste. Marie canals is nearly five times the tonnage through the Welland canal and over eight times that through the St. Lawrence canals; and that the United States coastal shipping is over eight times that of the Canadian through those canals.
The United States government is deepening the channel from the Detroit river up to lake Superior at very high cost-a cost comparable to that of the St. Lawrence seaway itself-and this waterway is to be toll free. It so happens that where United States tonnage is heavy on the whole waterway the tolls are free, and where our tonnage is heavier tolls are to be levied. I am not an economist, but I would expect this will produce an unbalanced economy to Canada's disadvantage in our great lakes system.
Thus far I have assumed that the Canadian government has decided on tolls. I am personally against tolls, particularly on the Welland canal, but in saying this I know I am in the minority in this house. There are so many implications in connection with the imposition of tolls that I proposed that the Canadian government should have an economic 
survey made before tolls are applied. I thought such a survey might come up with findings on the impact tolls might have on our economy and provide a better answer than a tolls committee, which would have little time for such a survey and which might be primarily interested in seeing what the traffic could bear.
Many plants have settled in the Toronto and Hamilton area and along the Welland canal. They established in those areas never expecting tolls, and their operations are geared to a toll free economy. I will take the paper industry for example. We have several paper mills in the Niagara district, and much of their pulpwood comes from the province of Quebec. The enlarged and deepened canal cannot help but result in their having to pay large sums of money for tolls without adding in any way to the economy of their operations. They must still continue to use small draught canal boats to gather up their pulpwood at the mouth of rivers of streams down which the pulpwood has been floated. The pulpwood is waterlogged and heavy, and no doubt they would be expected to pay tolls on the weight of wood containing nearly 50 per cent water.
A cord of wet wood weighs 5,000 pounds, and assuming a toll of 50 cents for bulk cargo this would mean paying a toll of $1.17 per cord, without taking into consideration the fact that in most cases a toll would be charged the ship when light on the return journey. Loads both ways cannot be carried by most ships, as the downbound or downstream tonnage is three and one half times the volume of the upbound or upstream tonnage.
I should like to go into some detail in *connection with the Ontario Paper Company at Thorold. This company has 1,200 employees and an annual payroll of $8 million. They have wood preparing plants and research facilities in Ontario. In addition the company owns a plant at Baie Comeau in Quebec on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river where it has its own power and wood preparing plants. The company also owns a fleet of 11 ships engaged in transporting not only its own products but general commerce as well. Altogether this company has 7,910 permanent and seasonal employees, with a total annual payroll of $25,700,000. Its total production amounts to over $60 million, of which $58 million was exported to the United States; and this is equivalent to 2.3 per cent of Canada's total exports to that country.
The Ontario Paper Company has always treated labour most fairly. I think this company's contribution and that of its top

executives is a fine example of responsible Canadian industry. The company presented a brief to the tolls committee of the St. Lawrence seaway authority not long ago, and I wish to quote part of that brief, as follows:
The locational advantage of proximity to its power source is now being threatened if the Ontario hydroelectric power commission carries out its policy of applying power rates on a system-wide basis rather than based on cost of transmission of power from close sources. If. in addition, a burden of $800,000 per year for tolls upon its traffic is superimposed upon it, it could be the means of forcing the location into an untenable position, thus forcing consideration of either abandonment or relocating its manufacturing equipment to a location where we have our own power facilities and avoiding the burden of tolls.
Based on press reports from Washington and Ottawa concerning tolls, the company is now of the opinion that the tolls could result in an additional expenditure of more than $1 million a year on their part. If the Ontario Paper Company finds it necessary to relocate because of these extra burdens- that is, their higher cost of power and the proposed seaway tolls-it will be a tremendous loss to the Niagara district and to the province of Ontario. I cannot think that this government or any tolls committee would want to see this happen. The building of the waterway will not in any way add to the economy of this company's operations.
I am of the opinion that the Welland canal should not be put in the same category as the St. Lawrence seaway. We should all strive for a closer-knit economy in Canada. Last year when the Minister of Transport was in Hamilton he was reported in the press as having assured the people there that they would be able to purchase coal shipped from Nova Scotia. If high toll charges are placed on the St. Lawrence seaway it will be difficult for Nova Scotia coal to compete with United States coal in the cities of Hamilton and Toronto.
There is one other important point. I have often heard reports to the effect that the operation of the canals is to be under a joint committee of Canada and the United States. *The canals have been very well operated under the Department of Transport, and I would like to see their operation continue on this basis and not placed under any other supervision.

maintopic: TOLLS CHARGED ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing as I do a riding that does not actually border the Welland canal but is in close proximity to it, I feel duty bound to say a word on this important question. Before doing so I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Welland on his very fine presentation of the question, 57071-3-74i
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls and to state categorically that I am in full and complete agreement with what he said.
In my opinion the question of tolls for the Welland canal is one of the most important questions facing not only the people of the Niagara district but the people of Canada. It is one that must be answered by the government of Canada in the very near future. Without doubt there will be a lot of public opinion both pro and con on this important subject. If tolls are imposed on the Welland canal they will work a hardship on industry, and especially those long-established industries which have done so much in the past to protect our national economy and to preserve our independence and freedom. These industries will indeed be placed at an economic disadvantage.
Tolls are imposed only for the use of facilities constructed for special purposes, such as locks built in various places for the floating of logs on isolated inland streams. I admit this is more true in the United States than in Canada, but I feel that tolls should not be charged for the use of improvements in Canada that are generally available for navigation and commerce. Some stretches of the connecting channels between the great lakes in both the United States and Canada have been improved by our engineers, and this has been going on for over 50 years without any suggestion of tolls. Over the years it has been absolutely shown that the canal free of tolls is a stimulus to commerce and generates new business for forms of transportation other than those directly using the canal. Herbert Hoover once said:
New waterways are not competitive but complementary to our great and efficient railways. It is the history of transportation that an increase of facilities and a cheapening of transportation increases the volume of traffic.
One must agree that ultimately tolls are always paid by the consumer, whether he knows it or not. They are included in the cost of transportation and eventually wind up in the price charged for the product. In the case of our basic materials the added cost of transportation through tolls increases in proportion to the number of processes through which the material passes before it finally goes off the dealer's shelves. It is thus cheaper, to say nothing of less painful, for all of us to pay for waterway improvements just once through taxes rather than repeatedly through the higher prices which would result from tolls on the Welland canal.
We must never forget that our improved canal, free of tolls, will play an important role in the defence of our nation. Opening up the great lakes by means of the St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland canal
1164	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls means opening up ship-building facilities around the lakes for the construction of seagoing vessels in time of emergency. It also means a safe lane a thousand miles long for the shipment of war materials, thus shortening the hazardous voyage across the Atlantic by nearly one-third.
Surely no one will argue that you should expect tolls to pay for this defence measure. It requires no stretch of the imagination to picture the hullabaloo that would be raised if tolls were proposed, say for instance, in New York harbour. Surely one must have his tongue in his cheek if he goes out and actually campaigns for tools on the Welland canal. To me they certainly are vulnerable, and I hope it will not start a landslide which will clog our canal and spill over into avenues of commerce which have contributed so much to the growth and economic welfare of our nation.
To my way of thinking those fighting for high tolls overlook two important facts. The first is the expansion in foreign trade which the canal will generate, and the other is the tremendous growth of population not only in our own province and dominion but in the United States as well.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, from engineers who have made an estimate of the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence seaway that the traffic to be expected through the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence seaway would be somewhere in the vicinity of 35 million to 37 million tons. Other engineers and businessmen tell us that the estimate for 1965 would be well over 52 million tons. Perhaps the more pessimistic observers and engineers say that it will increase to only 40 million tons.
I contend that it is not possible to charge a toll in the Niagara district without causing drastic harm to the economy of our nation. One cannot help but submit that the St. Lawrence seaway is faced with a dilemma, and certainly the only solution is a low toll which will not be injurious to industry but will be helpful to industry in the Niagara district.
I realize that the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act provides that if tolls are imposed they may be charged in two ways; either by a toll system set up by the St. Lawrence seaway authority alone for the Canadian section of the canal, or by a joint toll system set up by the St. Lawrence seaway authority together with the American seaway development corporation, which the Minister of Transport tells us will be meeting about July 1. Naturally their findings would have to be approved by the governments of


Canada and the United States, and would constitute an international agreement binding upon both countries.
Many organizations, chambers of commerce, the Hamilton council and the Toronto council and various councils in the Niagara district have at times recommended to the Minister of Transport that the Welland canal be maintained as a toll free system. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that any toll system reduces the potential of the Welland canal to provide maximum benefits not only for all the people of the Niagara district but of Canada as well. The collection of even a minimum toll would work hardship in many cases, and affect the ability of industry and agriculture to expand.
Back in 1934, Mr. Speaker, there was a full debate in this house on the motion that all goods shipped through canals owned and operated by the government of Canada be subject to taxation. In speaking against this motion Hon. R. J. Manion, at that time minister of railways and canals, stated in part:
In regard to the Panama, Suez and Manchester canals, it is true that they collect tolls. We must realize, however, that the conditions under which these canals are operated are altogether different from those existing in connection with Canadian canals. The Manchester canal is a private commercial enterprise, whereas in Canada our canals are national. Then the Suez canal is operated by a privately owned company. True, the Panama canal is publicly owned and operated, but we must remember this important point; the difference between the Suez, the Panama and our Canadian canals is that no vessel-owner is forced to use either the Suez or the Panama.
On the other hand, in Canada we have no alternative water route from the western grain fields, unless one wishes to use the railways from the head of the lakes. As has already been pointed out, however, the railroad would be so much higher that it would not be possible in the marketing of grain. It is important that we should have the lowest possible rates in order that we may compete with countries whose grain fields are closer to the seaboards than are the fields of Canada.
To me, Mr. Speaker, those words are as true today as they were in 1934, and perhaps more so, and I think today they even assume a broader aspect since this nation is more truly a trading nation, with its prosperity depending in large measure upon sound competitive business in our world trade.
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. When the United States agreed to join with Canada in the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway they did so only on the understanding that tolls were to be collected to cover the cost of construction, maintenance and operation of what Washington certainly regarded as the seaway proper, that is the section of the St. Lawrence river lying between Iroquois, Ontario and Montreal. I do not believe there was ever in Washington's mind any idea that

the heretofore toll free Welland ship canal, completed in 1932 at a cost of well over $130 million, would be included in the St. Lawrence seaway for toll purposes. I certainly hope that Washington is still under that impression, and that it is their disposition that the matter of tolls on the existing Welland ship canal is one for Canada alone to decide.
I believe they gained this attitude owing partly to the fact that the Welland ship canal has always been under the control of the Minister of Transport. I can only repeat with emphasis that it should remain under the control of the Minister of Transport rather than the St. Lawrence seaway authority. The Toronto board of trade, the Hamilton chamber of commerce, and several other bodies representing the whole public community are very anxious that no change be made in the present set-up. I agree with them just as strongly as possible that the Welland ship canal should stay under the control of the Minister of Transport, and should continue to be toll free.
We cannot forget that the Canadian and United States users of the Welland ship canal started their shipping through that canal on a toll free basis nearly a quarter of a century before a start was made on the present St. Lawrence seaway. Certainly the present users of the Welland ship canal did not ask that it be deepened to 27 feet to conform to the seaway standard. They have been and are still quite content with the existing 25-foot depth. They have all built their ships to conform to this depth. It is hard to conceive, at least in my estimation, why they should now be expected to bear the cost of a deeper channel for which they did not ask and which will not be of any service to them.
I cannot help but wonder whether Windsor and Detroit would like to pay tolls on iron ore, limestone, scrap and other cargoes which move through the Sault canal and the St. Clair and St. Marys rivers. One only has to think how much worse off Toronto, Hamilton, Welland and the Niagara district generally would be and, indeed, our neighbouring and satellite communities, in the event of tolls on the Sault canal, tolls on the three connecting rivers and tolls on the Welland ship canal. You can well appreciate why we in the Niagara-Toronto area are so exercised about the evil potentialities, not only for ourselves who reside in the district but for all those in Ontario who will be so seriously affected by such a move.
Certainly cargo tolls on the Sault canal and the Detroit, St. Clair and St. Marys rivers would constitute double jeopardy for those Canadian industries, including the prairie
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls wheat grower, forced to use those facilities as well as the Welland ship canal. In my estimation the only way we can avoid the numerous troubles that seem to be ahead of us is for Ottawa to understand fully the many and serious implications of imposing tolls on cargoes passing through the Welland ship canal.
May I sum up by saying first, Mr. Speaker, that to establish tolls on the Welland ship canal would create a dangerous precedent which would hamper the future development of the great lakes area and place undue restrictions on Canada's economic growth. Second, tolls would divert trade from the water route, resulting in removing the stabilizing influence of water transport on other forms of transportation. Above everything else, Mr. Speaker, we should not lose sight of the point that any agreement with the United States pertaining to tolls would take control of the canal out of Canadian hands, as it would be subject to joint control.
Many of our existing industries have invested huge sums of money in the region of the Welland canal based upon free water transportation, and certainly this investment would be confiscated by oppressive tolls. I think we here in Canada should take the stand, and it should be a firm one indeed, that the purpose of the seaway is to attract industries, not to destroy them or drive them away. Our country can advance in wealth and power at a wonderful rate but it would be tragic indeed if this generation, possessing economic resources never before equalled, were to have such tolls imposed upon them.
May I make this statement, and I make it with no feeling of ill will whatsoever toward the United States. I say that the United States is looking after the interests of the United States and not those of Canada. I say they realize that if we suddenly start charging tolls on the Welland ship canal certainly United States cities such as Baltimore, Maryland, and others will get the business rather than Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor or the Niagara area, because freight would naturally move by an alternative allAmerican route. It is all right to argue that tolls are charged on the Panama and Suez canals, but we cannot lose sight of the fact that ships actually make money by paying these tolls.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that as members of the House of Commons we should stand squarely on our own feet with regard to the toll question, because we need the western and the great lakes business. It is my sincere hope that the Minister of Transport will be able to bring a favourable reply to the house indicating that tolls will not

St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls be charged on the Welland canal. We are looking to him to that end. I say with emphasis, Mr. Speaker, that to charge tolls on the Welland ship canal would be a step backward so far as the future of this country is concerned.

maintopic: TOLLS CHARGED ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with keen interest to the two speeches just made by the hon. members for Welland and Niagara Falls. Both have indicated clearly that while they are in favour of the principle of tolls on the St. Lawrence seaway they do not favour the application of tolls on the Welland canal. It is easy for any member of the house to understand why these two and perhaps other members representing areas in the Niagara peninsula are fearful of the effects which tolls may have on established industries in those areas.
The reason I rise is to discuss the problem generally and also to regret the fact, first, that the Minister of Transport is not in his seat-he is detained, I am sure, by other important business-and, second, to complain about the fact that the minister and the government have not seen fit to alleviate some of the fears and anxieties of those groups in the country which will be affected by the imposition of tolls. In fact there has been very little said either by the minister or the government on the question of tolls since they took office following the election of June 10 last year.
It is unfortunate that that should be the case, because while I know that in the earlier period after assumption of office by the government it was difficult to deal with a problem of this nature. Nevertheless as time went on, and particularly in the last few months, it has in my opinion become much easier for a statement to be made either by the minister or the government in this respect.
As I understand it, sir, there are two groups agitating with reference to the question of tolls. First of all there is a group which would have no tolls at all on the seaway. They argue that tolls were imposed years ago on Canadian canals and were afterwards withdrawn, arguing therefrom that they were not a success and that on this occasion, following the opening of the seaway or shortly before, a toll system should not be instituted. Then there is another group, congregated mostly in the United States, agitating in favour of tolls which would be so prohibitive as to discourage traffic up and down the seaway.
It would appear to me, sir, that the attitude adopted by the St. Lawrence seaway authority, namely that of proceeding through a


committee in Canada and an opposite committee in the United States to establish a toll which is fair and reasonable, is the attitude which is commendable on this occasion. I should like to preface what I have to say now by stating that by international agreement, by legislation in this house and by pronouncements made both in this house and outside, the intention has been clear all along, that tolls should be charged on the St. Lawrence seaway.
The toll problem, of course, is a difficult and complicated one. It is made more difficult because of legislative requirements both in Canada and the United States that the project shall be self-liquidating. The operating costs, interest and amortization charges must be recovered from the tolls to be charged the users of these facilities. In other words the seaway is to be not only a self-liquidating project but a self-liquidating public utility.
As I said earlier and as was also said by the two hon. members who have just spoken, tolls were charged on canals in Canada in 1903. Those tolls were suspended for a time as an experiment, and afterwards were completely removed. They were completely removed because the United States decided to build the Erie canal and thereby take traffic from the upper regions of the great lakes down through that canal to the port of New York. Canada, finding itself losing traffic because of that canal, decided to remove tolls on its own canals entirely, and that proved to be successful. These tolls were finally abolished in 1905.
Now may I say a word about the basis for the establishment of tolls. The basis is briefly this. Capital expenditures are being incurred by both Canada and the United States in building the seaway. When the project is completed there will be an aggregate amount representing the capital cost of the seaway. It is on this amount that interest will accrue, and which must be amortized over a period of 50 years. Ift addition there will be the annual operating costs, including maintenance, but by far the greater part of the total costs will be the interest and amortization. Once the annual costs to be charged against the seaway have been determined there is another step which is of importance, and it is the consideration of the actual tariff of tolls.
What is the toll which is to be charged on the seaway? Before establishing a toll on the seaway I think one has to look at what is being done elsewhere, on the Panama canal and the Suez canal, for instance. It is only natural that one should compare the operations of these two canals. The Panama canal, for instance, can be easily bypassed. In other

words a ship going through the Panama canal need not come back by the same route. As a result the authorities operating the Panama canal see to it that light vessels are charged only 80 per cent of the toll on loaded vessels. The situation is not the same with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway. It cannot be bypassed. Once a ship enters the St. Lawrence seaway it must go through and must come back. It cannot go by another route. It need not, of course, go through the whole route up to the head of the lakes and back, but it must retrace its route after it has entered the seaway at the St. Lambert lock at Montreal in order to come out of the seaway.
Then again, in the case of the St. Lawrence seaway there is another factor which does not operate in either the Panama or the Suez canals. In Canada there are other paralleling transportation facilities along the seaway route; there are here parallel highway and railway facilities offering competition to the water route. Canada agreed to the imposition of tolls by international understanding. Until the month of March, 1947, I do not believe there had been any thought in Canada of imposing tolls on the seaway; but when it became clear that Canada was able, willing and anxious to go ahead with the building of the seaway the United States became apprehensive lest it would have no voice in a seaway which would be used by a large proportion of United States shipping. A statement by the secretary of state for external affairs was made at the time in the House of Commons on that subject. His statement, on April 24, 1947, is recorded at page 2354 of Hansard as follows:
The Canadian government has now concurred in principle with the proposal to make the St. Lawrence seaway self-liquidating by means of toll charges subject to the conclusion of arrangements satisfactory to both governments for the implementation of this principle.
This statement was repeated to the United States government in 1951 by an exchange of notes, I believe, and if not certainly by other correspondence, which pointed out particularly that Canada merely approved the principle of tolls. I emphasize this because of what I intend to say a little later. Canada merely approved the principle of tolls, without making any reference to the extent of the work to be amortized, the division of expenditures between the two countries, or to the allocation of costs as between power and navigation.
Then again the same idea is contained in certain sections of the seaway authority act. From the legislation it is clear that if tolls are to be established by agreement between Canada and the United States, directions pertaining to such tolls must be given by the
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls governor in council. Then the seaway authority act clearly sets out the purpose of the tolls. The tolls must, first of all, be fair and reasonable. Tolls must be high enough to recover the capital costs of the seaway, and they must be low enough to encourage traffic along the seaway. It would be ridiculous to make tolls so high that the cost of moving ships through the seaway would be prohibitive.
As I have said, in accordance with the act the tolls must be fair and reasonable. Furthermore, they must be non-discriminatory. Tolls must encourage increased utilization of the navigation facilities; for it would be anathema, as I have said, to spend $300 million or more to improve these facilities between Montreal and lake Erie only to impose prohibitive tolls.
Now, the point which I am sure interests the two hon. members who have just taken their seats, and the house in general, is this. What are to be the amounts of the tolls? This is a very difficult and complicated decision to make. A careful study would seem to indicate that there should be, first of all, a low toll on the net registered tonnage of the vessel applicable to all loaded or unloaded ships, and next a toll on the cargo itself. For example, if one were to encounter a ship having a net registered tonnage of 10,000 tons, and if there were say a toll of 10 cents per ton on that net registered tonnage, the ship would pay $1,000. If, over and above that, the ship had a cargo of 20,000 tons, assuming a toll of 50 cents per ton the ship would pay an additional $10,000, and hence on a 20,000-ton cargo a toll of $11,000 would be imposed. This is a simple method of assessing tolls. It should not be complicated like railway freight tariffs, because if it were then it would become extremely difficult of application and in case of appeal on complaints by shippers.
However, as I said earlier and as I repeat now, this is a matter for the tolls committees of both Canada and the United States to determine. It is, as I said at the outset, unfortunate that the minister has given the house little or no information on this extremely important matter. The house is entitled to know something about these tolls, as well as the shippers and ship operators who will be affected. I am sorry to say that the minister has not made very many pronouncements on the subject. I believe I am accurate in stating that on one occasion he went to a dominion marine association convention, not far from here, and made a statement on the subject, and that was quite some time ago. Apart from that there has been no statement on the subject at all. On the contrary, there has been a considerable

St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls amount of information emanating from the United States, to which I think this house and the country were entitled. For instance, on May 14 there was a statement emanating from the chairman of the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation, the United States entity, that tolls would be made public on July 1.
On the same day the hon. member for Welland asked the Minister of Transport, although he did not know about the statement from Washington, what the decision was with reference to the Canada-United States tolls committee. The hon. member was told that no decision had yet been reached, and that a public announcement would be made when such decision was reached.
The next day the minister was asked if he had seen the statement made on that same day by the president of the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, or whether he was aware of that statement. His reply was that he had nothing to add, that no decision had been arrived at.
Meanwhile, on May 17, the chairman of the United States tolls committee, Mr. Reese Harill, who has already been referred to in this debate, announced in effect the amount the tolls would be, and I would like to give his statement to the house again because it does bear on this subject. I quote from the Financial Post of May 17, 1958, bearing the dateline Washington, D.C., as follows:
In so far as the actual tolls are concerned the United States toll committee chairman still says, "We'll not be too far off from the target of $1.25 per ton for general cargo and .50 cents per ton for bulk."
Then, ten days later, there is a statement emanating from Ottawa confirming everything which has come out of Washington thus far, both the statement made by the chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation and the United States chairman of the tolls committee, to the effect that this is what is under discussion, that this is what is being considered, and that a statement would be made on the matter about July 1. My grievance at this time is first of all, that these statements, instead of emanating from Washington, should have emanated from Ottawa concurrently. My complaint is that there are many questions in respect of this matter which should not have been left unanswered. For instance, how will the tolls affect different commodities? Will certain commodities or certain classes of traffic receive more favourable rates than others? Will there be any discrimination in tolls as between Canadian and United States traffic or between local
[Mr. Chevrier.l
and overseas traffic? What are the latest estimates of traffic on the seaway?
There have been several estimates given as to traffic. In 1954 the United States estimates gave a figure of around 36J million tons. They were revised afterwards to somewhere between 30 and 35 million tons. Then there are the estimates made by the Department of Trade and Commerce away back in 1940 or 1944 which indicated the traffic potential at that time to be about 44J million tons and there are also the estimates made by the economists of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. But all these estimates may well be obsolete by now. These are estimates which were announced months ago, as a matter of fact, several years ago, and I think it would be well if this house and the country were told what are the latest estimates of traffic on the seaway and particularly what are the latest estimates of the cost of the seaway, because it is clear that no toll policy can be established unless the costs and the anticipated traffic are correlated, unless the costs and the traffic can be gauged as closely to the actual as is possible to gauge them.
Then there is the all-important question of how and where tolls are to be collected. Should they be collected separately from the United States or jointly with the United States? There is no provision covering this point in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act and it would seem to me that it would be a mistake to have two agencies collecting tolls, one a Canadian agency and the other a United States agency, because not only would that be a nuisance to the shipper but it would be a difficult thing from the point of view of accounting. It would be far simpler, since Canada is paying two-thirds of the cost of the seaway and since ships must of necessity enter the soaway in Canada through the St. Lambert canal at Montreal, that one agency and one agency alone be entrusted with the collection of tolls. I hope it will be found that that agency will be the St. Lawrence seaway authority. I am sure that they could make some sort of agreement, and I hope that they will if it has not already been done, with the St. Lawrence development corporation, the United States entity, that they would on behalf of both groups collect the tolls and then turn over the United States portion to the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation.
As to the points of collection, St. Lambert in the Lachine section and Welland in the upper section seem to be the logical locations for collection of tolls and when the volume of traffic reaches the point where navigational facilities become necessary at Cornwall, then

it would seem that Cornwall should be an additional point for collection of tolls. That is why I repeat that it is unfortunate that the minister has not seen fit to enlighten the house or the country on these matters and I hope he will take the first opportunity to do so.
Two hon. members who have just spoken have touched on a very important question, namely that of whether or not tolls should be charged on the Welland canal. Certainly from what I have said thus far and from the understanding made by the two governments, it would appear that in the year 1951, when the legislation was passed, the intention at that time was to cover the Welland canal. However, there was information which I am sure the seaway authority did not have and could not possibly have envisaged when the house was considering the over-all picture. Here again I must say that while the house gave unanimous consent to this legislation back in those years I am sure there are many members of parliament who would not have approved the project if they had not been assured by the government of the day that this was to be a self-liquidating project.
I return to the question of the Welland canal. When the legislation was passed, and for quite a long time afterwards, it was envisaged that the Welland canal would involve an expenditure of only $2 million. That was the estimate as it was tabled in the house at that time; in other words, in order to deepen Welland from 25 to 27 feet the estimate of cost was $2 million. That certainly could not be considered by any stretch of the imagination as being a large amount having regard to the total cost of $300 million which was being voted at the time. So that even at that time the amount of tolls with reference to the Welland canal, having regard to the total amount of the expenditure, could only have been a very small amount. It now turns out, unfortunately, that the cost-and I am sure that is nobody's fault-of the work in the Welland canal will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30 million. That could not have been envisaged at the time because it was only when the contractors and engineers got into the field at Welland that they discovered a large portion of the work in connection with dredging would have to be done in rock. The dredging in rock will be far more costly, and I am informed will be in the neighbourhood of $15 to $16 per cubic yard as compared with $2 or $2.50 per cubic yard for ordinary earth or clay dredging. I stand to be corrected on these amounts for I am speaking from memory only.
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls
The point I am trying to make is that it was not envisaged at the time that this additional amount of $28 million would be expended at Welland, and now that it has to be expended this may well make the difference in support of, and in substantiation of the claim made by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) and the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) that the operation of that canal should be exempted from the imposition of tolls.
There is another factor. Section 15 of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act provided,
I believe, for a situation such as this. Section 15 states, in subsection 3, that every such tariff-that is, tariff of tolls-or amendment thereto shall be filed with the board of transport commissioners and shall become operative from the date of such filing. Then subsection 4, which I think is extremely important, says:
Any person interested may at any time file a complaint with the board of transport commissioners that there is unjust discrimination in an existing tariff and the board shall thereupon consider such complaint and make a finding thereon which shall be reported to the authority.
The point I am trying to make is this: that if an industry on the Welland canal feels itself aggrieved by the imposition of these tolls, high or low though they may be, it may make application to the board of transport commissioners by way of complaint and be heard under that section of the act. That section envisages that where there is unjust discrimination in a tariff the board would thereupon act to remove such discrimination. While I have no time or desire to go into the reasons which may impell the board to act in cases such as this, I think the board of transport commissioners would apply to these rates the same arguments as they apply with reference to unjust discrimination in so far as other rates that are considered under the Railway Act. There is much jurisprudence on this subject-many legal cases-and, in fact, a number of recommendations were made in the report of Mr. Justice Turgeon on freight rates which was tabled in the house some years ago and which dealt with this question of unjust discrimination.
Thus I say that while the position on the Welland canal may be different from that of other areas along the seaway route in that there were no industries along the other canals in the beginning; it was built either in the existing waters or alongside the shores or inland on farm territory where no industry was then in existence; though since then, in certain areas, industries have sprung up. The position with reference to Welland, is that the industries along the Welland canal have been established there for many years and it may well be that they would have a case in

St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls arguing that the toll which the seaway authorities would establish would be one that is discriminatory with regard to their industry.
Then again there is also the obligation of the government under the seaway authority act. After the tolls committees of both countries have agreed upon a tariff of tolls, following study and examination to recommend to their respective governments; it is then up to the governments to determine whether that toll shall apply along the whole seaway.
The government has the right, if it so desires, under the order in council which it will pass, if it so wishes, to exempt a certain portion of the route from the operation of the toll, and it would seem to me that this could hardly be done without consultation with the seaway authority and with the other government. In other words, it becomes clear from what has been said in this debate that there are two members of parliament who are apprehensive lest the industries in their area be detrimentally affected. The government, I respectfully submit, should look into this matter and give consideration to the points made by the two members that industries may be injuriously affected on the Welland canal. Should these apprehensions prove well founded, consideration should be given to whether or not sufficient relief can be given to these industries under section 15 of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act. I, certainly, would have thought so when the act was introduced in the house. It may be, because of the changed conditions which I outlined a moment ago, that the position is not the same today, but that is a matter for study. Then it would seem to me that consideration should be given to whether or not the Welland canal should be exempted from the application of the tariff of tolls.
It is impossible to answer this question, in my opinion, unless a study has been made of the whole situation by the proper body to do so, the tolls committee and the seaway authority. That is why, some time ago, in an earlier debate, I recommended the establishment-and I have done so on more than one occasion-of an economic survey to consider the whole effect of the seaway on the various regions of Canada and, of course, to study this question as well.
I conclude by repeating what I said at the outset of my remarks, that the question of a tariff of toll is an extremely difficult and complicated one. It is one which I am sure will be given careful study by the St. Lawrence seaway authority and it is one which no doubt the government will wish to consider carefully before it imposes a tariff of tolls which will apply, as the law now obtains, from one end of the seaway to the other. It will, of course, be the prerogative of the


government to exempt from the operation of the tolls the seaway route or any part of it.
I am sure that in view of the international agreement and in the light of other statements I have made, the government will have sortie difficulty in arriving at that conclusion. But I am sure all of us here-and I want to emphasize this-would not want to see these tremendous sums of money spent and then see the establishment of a toll which would be prohibitive. I am sure the St. Lawrence seaway authority does not want this, and I am sure the authority is going to do its utmost and bend over backwards to see to it that the toll will be so attractive as to encourage traffic. I also feel that should the case be such that because of the high costs of the seaway as compared with the amount of traffic that will go through it tolls must of necessity be high in order to amortize the principal, then I think the government should give careful consideration to refinancing part of the indebtedness so that shipping may be encouraged to move through the route.
I have not looked at the cost figures for a long time nor have I had an opportunity to study them. In fact, I do not know what the latest figures are. I have seen the budget tabled in the house but those figures are not necessarily the figures that will be agreed upon between the two governments and therefore I am not in a position to state what the capital expenditure is at this time. But what I do say is that having regard to this great international enterprise I am confident both the seaway authority and the government will want to make sure the toll will be of such a nature that ships will move freely through the seaway.

Mr. Speaker, if the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) is going to raise another subject perhaps I should say a few words on the grievance before us. The government, of course, had no inkling that this question- of tolls on the St. Lawrence seaway would be raised this afternoon and unfortunately the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) under whose jurisdiction this matter comes is unable to be here. However, I can assure hon. members of the house that the officials of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the minister and the officials of his department have been giving very careful

consideration to this question and will continue to do so in an attempt to work out a reasonable, sensible solution.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who has had a great deal of experience because of the important post he held as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, has made a very interesting review this afternoon and he has pointed out just how complicated and difficult the question of tolls will be. Perhaps it is to be regretted that he did not get that problem settled before he left the seaway authority. It has not yet been settled, of course, but I can assure him and the other two hon. members who have spoken that a most careful study is being made of this subject and their suggestions will be given every consideration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to raise as the subject of a grievance the important question of what I consider to have been the interference of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) last Friday in connection with a television interview with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. By raising this matter on orders of the day I hoped the Prime Minister might give a satisfactory explanation of press and radio reports which appeared over the weekend concerning this event but as I understand the Prime Minister's explanation the best that can be said for it is that it adds to the confusion which already exists with regard to it.
This is not the first time that the Prime Minister by attempting to interpret statements which have been made previously in the press regarding remarks of his own and others with whom he was associated has created confusion of this kind. Far from clarifying the situations the Prime Minister's interpretations have made them even more difficult to understand. I am thinking of the 15 per cent trade diversion proposal and the clarification that has been attempted since. I am thinking also of the press conference of the secretary general of NATO and the interpretations that were given by the Prime Minister of the words of the secretary general of NATO and the interpretations of interpretations after that.
Last Friday we on this side of the house read with some surprise a report to the effect that the Prime Minister of Canada intervened in connection with a television interview that had been arranged between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. The Prime 57071-3-75i
16. 1958	1171
Television Interview-Alleged Interference Minister's reply to my question on the subject seems to me to be entirely unsatisfactory and certainly in direct divergence to the reports concerning it that have appeared not only in one newspaper but in a number of newspapers and over the air. In attempting to explain away this matter this afternoon the Prime Minister said we were attempting to make a mountain out of a molehill.

speechtext:
Well, we will see about that. The Prime Minister said that last Friday he and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom met representatives of the C.B.C. following their conference. Just before the arranged interview commenced the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, according to the Prime Minister of Canada, asked what would be the questions in this interview. The Prime Minister said this afternoon that as he recalled it the first of the two questions-and these were questions to be addressed not to the Prime Minister of Canada but to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

was whether or not the free trade proposal advanced last September would be on the agenda of the trade conference this fall. Our Prime Minister said this afternoon-and I think I am quoting accurately what he said- "I then said, 'No, no.' " That terminated the matter so far as he was concerned, the Prime Minister said today.
That may have terminated the matter so far as the Canadian Prime Minister was concerned but that explanation does not terminate the matter so far as we on this side of the house are concerned, it does not remove our strong feeling on the question of intervention or interference with the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by members of the government. We feel the Prime Minister should regard this in the same light we do in view of a debate which took place in this house only a year or so ago and which I will mention in more detail in a few minutes relating to intervention or interference with the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the part of members of the government. "No, no", said the Prime Minister.
What was the result of this "no, no"? Well, in this interview with Mr. Macmillan no question regarding the free trade offer was in fact asked. The matter was not brought up although it was one of the two questions, apparently, that the C.B.C. representative had in his mind and he had mentioned them to the man whom he was going to interview. Then when the Prime Minister gave his explanation this afternoon I, in order to give him another opportunity to clear up the

Television Interview-Alleged Interference matter, repeated my earlier question in somewhat different form. I said:
Arising out of the Prime Minister's answer, am 1 to understand that the statement attributed to him, not by one but by a number of reputable newspaper correspondents, "No, no, you cannot ask that question'-
And that was a quotation from the report in the press.
-then had nothing whatever to do with the question that Mr. Macmillan might have been asked by the C.B.C. reporter regarding free trade.
The Prime Minister said:
I have nothing really to add to what I have already said. Any question that arose was in consequence of his request as to the nature of the questions that were to be asked. In other words, he wanted to know in advance.
And when he was told in advance as to what one of the questions would be the Prime Minister himself admits that he intervened and said, "No, no." That seems to me to constitute interference in the affairs of the C.B.C. by the Prime Minister of this country, especially in view of the fact that in the subsequent interview no mention was made of this very important subject. May I just read what the Canadian Press had to say about this matter. This is the report which appeared throughout the country and it is substantiated by reports from other newspaper correspondents who were here on this occasion. This is the Canadian Press report of the incident as it appeared in the five o'clock edition of the Ottawa Journal of June 13, 1958:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker today intervened to prevent a C.B.C. interviewer from asking Prime Minister Macmillan of Britain a question about Britain's proposal for an Anglo-Canadian free trade area.
The C.B.C. asked Mr. Macmillan for a brief recorded television interview after he and Mr. Diefenbaker concluded a 45-minute discussion in the Canadian Prime Minister's office.
The interviewer explained to Mr. Macmillan before the actual recording began, that his first question would concern the British free trade proposal made last fall. He said-
That is the interviewer.
-the question would be: "Will Britain's free trade scheme be discussed at the commonwealth economic conference?"
Mr. Diefenbaker. standing beside Mr. Macmillan, said, "No, no," and a whispered conversation among the two prime ministers and the C.B.C. interviewer ensued.
When the recording began, the first and only question asked by the C.B.C. was what Mr. Macmillan considered the main achievements of his visit to Canada and the United States.
With great respect I suggest that nothing the Prime Minister said this afternoon in his ambiguous, cloudy and uncertain explanation relieves him from the responsibility of having intervened between the representative of the C.B.C. and the Prime Minister of

the United Kingdom in the way which determined, at least to some extent, the nature of the interview and the questions that would be asked. I claim that that is certainly interference in the affairs of the C.B.C.
Was there any justification for the Prime Minister in intervening in any way, shape or form in regard to a question addressed to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom about a free trade offer of his government made to the Canadian government last autumn? We on this side of the house have been trying to secure information on this matter for months in the place where that information should be secured, namely in the House of Commons, and we have not been successful. But we have read in accounts, in reports outside the house, in newspapers, that this offer of free trade still stands. That statement was made by the president of the board of trade some weeks ago when he was in Montreal. That statement was made by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom himself only the other day when he is reported as saying that the United Kingdom stands by her suggestion for an Anglo-Canadian free trade area. Mr. Macmillan emphasized that the proposal for free trade had been laid on the table by the United Kingdom and it was still there; the offer remained to be taken up in whole or in part. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, surely it was the natural thing for a C.B.C. television interviewer to do, to suggest to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom that that was to be one of the questions he would ask him, the most natural and reasonable thing in the world.
It seems to me there was no cause for the Prime Minister intervening in this question in any way, shape or form or for saying, "No, no" or, "no, no, no" whatever he might have had in mind in using this double negative. It was a perfectly proper question for an interviewer to ask the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, a question which deals with the matter of the greatest possible importance, a matter which has aroused the interest of the people of this country.
I suggest that quite apart from the reasonableness of the question itself, whatever the question may have been that was suggested to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister of Canada had no right whatever to interfere in any way in this matter. I suggest that in the intervention which he made last Friday he was exercising a form of direct censorship over the C.B.C. interviewer carrying out his job. The Prime Minister, of all people, should have been the very first to appreciate the impropriety of this. We on this side of the house

recall how last March 29 he and other members of his party in the house at that time so bitterly criticized the prime minister of that day for writing, not to a C.B.C. interviewer or a C.B.C. correspondent but to the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that he did not think very much of a particular program which had appeared. This was after the program had appeared, not before someone was going to ask somebody whether he could put a question on the air. At that time the Prime Minister said that this constituted very serious interference with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
If a complaint made in writing to the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, complaining about a program that had been delivered, constituted very serious interference with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, how can you describe the intervention of the Prime Minister on this occasion when a question was addressed by a C.B.C. interviewer to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom concerning a matter which is of very considerable interest and great importance to this country and which in fact that interviewer wished to ask and which in fact, as it happens, he did not ask because of this intervention? Perhaps I might read from the Prime Minister's own statement at that earlier time. The Prime Minister, in attacking the prime minister of the day because he wrote the letter I have mentioned, had this to say as found on page 2830 of Hansard of March 29, 1957:
This seems to me-
He is referring to Mr. St. Laurent's letter to the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
-an example of supercilious censoriousness that is not in keeping with the maintenance of freedom of speech within this country.
Then he went on to say:
To say that the Prime Minister has the right, or, indeed, that he can defend the right to communicate with the chairman of the C.B.C., with all the vast authority and prestige which the position of Prime Minister carries, is one of the most outrageous propositions that have ever been advanced in this house. It denies freedom of speech. It denies that the C.B.C. may broadcast programs which are not agreeable to the susceptibilities of the Prime Minister.
If the present Prime Minister felt that way a little over a year ago about a letter of complaint addressed to the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by the prime minister of that day, I wonder what he would say if he were on this side of the house if the prime minister of that day had interfered between an interviewer and the prime minister of the United Kingdom in an effort at least to direct what he would or
16. 1958	1173
Television Interview-Alleged Interference would not be asked. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had some even harsher things to say at that time and the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) also contributed his bit to this debate, the result of which', as some hon. members will recall, was a whole series of questions put on the order paper to be answered orally by every cabinet minister of that day asking each cabinet minister to get up and say whether he had ever intervened in any way, by letter or orally, with the C.B.C. to influence any of their programs.
My hon. friends opposite will remember that we stood up one after another and answered that question and the opposition of that day got a good deal of pleasure out of that procedure. Later in the same debate to which I have referred the Postmaster General, in making his contribution to the attack on the government of that day for what they called interference, interference after the event not before, had this to say as found at page 2838 of Hansard of March 29, 1957:
-it is the . . . duty of the Prime Minister to keep away from intervention in the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I quite agree that it is the duty of the Prime Minister to keep away from intervention in the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I can imagine no more gratuitous or dangerous form of intervention than to suggest to an interviewer of that corporation what he may or may not ask the prime minister of the United Kingdom in an interview which had been arranged with the prime minister of that country. Again, Mr. Speaker, with very great respect, the ambiguous explanation of the Prime Minister this afternoon, and that is putting it mildly, does not remove in any way, shape or form our grievance or our strong feeling that such intervention has taken place. That is why I venture to bring this grievance to the attention of the house. If the Prime Minister is tempted in the future to dictate who shall say what over the air I suggest that he might hesitate and repeat to himself words which he used on a less happy occasion last Friday, "No, no, no."

On this point of order, may I point out that the hon. member for Essex East is completely distorting the rules. He did not speak for himself, he spoke for the former government as a whole. Now, the fact that he says
