subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate did deny that statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Deny what statement?

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The statement made by the Prime Minister, who persisted in saying there was no denial; I will not accept any denial, says the Prime Minister. This is clearly contrary to the rules of the house, and is a practice in which the Prime Minister should not indulge.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Perhaps since I have been dragged in to this, I could say one word.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: You jumped in, head first.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: What I asserted was that there was a denial at the time, as Hansard will show. There was no interference by the government in respect of that broadcast.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I think that we are confusing two matters. I asked the hon. member for Essex East what words he felt should have been accepted. If it were a denial by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate of a statement made by him in his place that he had not interfered with the C.B.C., then I feel sure the Prime Minister would have been bound, and would have accepted the statement. But as I recall what transpired it was not a denial of what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said about himself. I think we can proceed, and perhaps restrain our susceptibilities in a matter of this kind where obviously things will be said which are within the normal course of party conflict, and which would not be acceptable on both sides of the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
To return once more to the trend of my thoughts, I was dealing with a subject, Mr. Speaker, which does lead to the wounding of the susceptibilities of my hon. friends opposite, namely the broadcast that was advertised to take place by Bernard Ostry. The people of Canada were interested in finding out what this author had to say. However, the government of that day had in its membership those who did not desire that the people of Canada should become aware of some of the things which had been dealt with in the book. At the time, there was a question raised as to who had actually brought about the cancellation of that much anticipated broadcast. We were unable to find out. The only information available was that information would not be given.

Television Interview-Alleged Interference
Then came the occasion mentioned by my hon. friend on the 26th, 27th and 28th of March last, in which there was again an example of the kind of thing which should not take place. In this case the then prime minister-I am not going into the facts because he is not in this house-heard a broadcast by a young professor in Winnipeg who referred to a subject that sometimes arouses the susceptibilities of the Leader of Opposition, namely the kind of policy that Canada had at the time of Suez when Canada, through the hon. gentleman, cast a vote against Britain and France and placed them in the same position as the U.S.S.R. as countries which had departed from the course that they should have followed.
This is one subject about which my hon. friends do not like to hear. On that occasion, the then prime minister wrote a letter in which he pointed out-at least we understand this is what the letter contained because we were never able to see it-that this young man, who had only been in Canada for a few months, did not have that background of understanding education or appreciation, to be able to speak to the Canadian people through the medium of the C.B.C. In other words, the direction was clear, that he should no longer appear as a commentator on the C.B.C. Now, those were the two examples that were brought to the attention of the house as examples of interference with the rights of the people of Canada to obtain information.
I now come to the matter in question. My hon. friend really revealed the reason why he is so exercised, because he said that they have not yet found out about the free trade offer. Might I suggest that he should bring up something new. They used all that during the election campaign-bring up something new. Get a new speech.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: You get a new one every day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
This was used over and over again during the election campaign. It was said that facts had been concealed. There was nothing concealed here. The question was asked as to whether or not this would be on the agenda. It was a joint interview and I was present on that occasion. The question of whether or not it would be discussed at the conference this fall is something which will have to be determined in due course. However, there was no concealment; members of the press gallery asked question after question regarding this matter and the prime minister answered them. There was certainly no concealment in so far as the C.B.C. keeping anything from the people was concerned. Last evening Mr. Edgar Mclnnis, the president of the council of the Canadian


institute of international affairs, interviewed the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and that interview was quite lengthy. There was nothing kept from the Canadian people; it was indeed a full and free discussion. I say that this simply indicates how short of issues are my hon. friends opposite when they endeavour to raise such matters in order to obscure the real issues facing this country.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Rubbish.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
My hon. friend is the
best judge in the house of rubbish.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I have listened to enough of it from the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I have nothing to withdraw. There was no interference with the C.B.C.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
My hon. friends have
suddenly developed an affection for the independence of that body which they did not have during their days in office, whereas we know today, as from day to day we listen to the broadcasts and the commentators, the C.B.C. is not under the same degree of control, whether by direct influence or whether it was subconscious in its effect, which brought about a situation in this country where some of the commentators did not enjoy the freedom they enjoy today, to speak fearlessly regardless of any circumstances. The former situation was made clear by the communication to the C.B.C. to the effect that a certain commentator had not spoken as he should have done and did not have a proper realization of Canadian conditions and that he had trodden on the delicate toes of the government then in power.
My hon. friend has spoken with exaggerated exuberance about this matter in his desire to leave the impression, which cannot be left with the Canadian people who have listened to the C.B.C. since June 21, 1957 and have heard day by day the broadcasts over the various channels of that body, that criticism has been restrained.
The government has at no time or in any way interfered with the C.B.C. When my hon. friend reads what I said in 1957 he will be aware of my views in this matter. I repeat my words, that as long as this government is in power-and that will be a long time if this kind of picayune criticism persists- there will be no interference, directly or indirectly, with the criticisms of commentators or others, nor will there be any interference with the right of the people of Canada to secure full information on any and every subject. I think it makes it clear that this has been the state of affairs since June 21 last,

when one remembers that the only example which could be raised by the opposition in no way indicates any interference with the C.B.C. The information in this case had already been given in detail to the press conference and had been broadcast over the C.B.C., in part or in full, and last evening the fullest possible discussion was allowed on this matter during the course of the interview of the prime minister by Mr. Mclnnis.
The only thing about it, Mr. Speaker, is that my hon. friends have harassed themselves because they do not have the information on the so-called free trade proposition which was advanced to this government, and they are adopting this method of bringing to the attention of the country that they have not been able to secure this information and so are endeavouring to hold this government responsible for interfering with the C.B.C., which is something it never has done, will not now do and does not intend to do.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has referred to this matter as being picayune and has given the impression that this is a mountain made out of a molehill. These were some of the words he used when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) today asked him some questions on the orders of the day. I am sure there are many precedents in speeches of the right hon. gentleman which clearly indicate that this is an important question. One is, I think, understandably surprised by the words of the Prime Minister, particularly in view of his well-known interest in matters affecting freedom in all its aspects, in that he should have regarded the raising of this particular question as not so important as is being suggested. One is certainly justified in saying that the Prime Minister is not doing himself justice, having in mind the views expressed in his capacity as a private member in other days.
The Prime Minister says this is a mountain made out of a molehill but he has gone further in the speech which he has just made. I suggest that this, as an explanation of what has already been said, only adds to the confused situation with respect to what the Prime Minister actually did say and does not clarify what he perhaps intended to convey. The Prime Minister's remarks on the orders of the day were recalled by the Leader of the Opposition but I think they deserve to be mentioned again. The Prime Minister said: "We discussed various matters, it being understood that thereafter there would be a joint conference before the C.B.C. When we came out we met the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation representatives, and just before the interview
16, 1958	1177
Television Interview-Alleged Interference commenced the Prime Minister asked what the questions were." He asked what the questions were and in this context, and in the words used by the Prime Minister that query by the British prime minister could only mean one thing, and that is: What questions are going to be put to me by those who are going to interview us? That interpretation, I say, is the only interpretation which can reasonably be made.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. gentleman what he is reading from?

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am reading the observations made by the Prime Minister during the course of this afternoon, observations already referred to by the Leader of the Opposition and commented on by the right hon. gentleman. I was saying that when the British prime minister asked what the questions were, in the context of the language used by the right hon. gentleman they could only mean that the British prime minister was thinking of only one thing, that is the questions that had been prepared, presumably by the C.B.C. for submission to the British prime minister for reply by him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: What does the hon. member mean, "prepared by the press"?

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
By the C.B.C., I should say. And now that the Prime Minister has raised this, it is a matter which touches not only the C.B.C., because, after all, although the C.B.C. is representative of radio and television it does represent the press in the larger sense of the word, and this is certainly a matter which can be considered as involving not only the freedom of radio and television but also the freedom of the press itself.
The Prime Minister went on, in answer to the Leader of the Opposition, as I recall it to say: "The first question on the list of two was whether or not the representation or the so-called proposal advanced last September regarding free trade with the United Kingdom would be on the agenda of the trade conference this fall, and I said 'no, no' ". Now that answer, that observation when related to the previous sentence of the right hon. gentleman, certainly presents a picture in which it is clear what happened. Certain questions were put by the representatives of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the British prime minister and, for some reason, which has been made manifest not only on Friday last but for many months, the Prime Minister seemingly is reluctant to have any unnecessary mention made of this proposal which was brought forward, first of all, by the chancellor of the exchequer last
1178	HOUSE OF
Television Interview-Alleged Interference autumn and more recently, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, by the president of the board of trade three or four weeks ago in Montreal.
The Prime Minister may have good reasons for not wanting this opinion of the British proposal discussed. After all, the Prime Minister has access as leader of the government to information not open to those of us on this side of the house. But he could at least give reasons for minimizing the number of occasions when this question could be discussed. But in the absence of a satisfactory explanation, it is the duty of the opposition to ascertain from the government and from the Prime Minister what its attitude with regard to this proposal is.
The Prime Minister obviously minimizes the importance of the British proposal. Today he does not even call it a proposal; he says it is "a so-called proposal". That is not what the chancellor of the exchequer said. That is not what Sir David Eccles, president of the board of trade said; that is not what Mr. Harold Macmillan said in the press conference he gave the other day. We mean business with this proposal put forward by Her Majesty's government, said the British prime minister. It is not a so-called proposal. I know the right hon. gentleman is seeking to minimize his own proposal of last July with regard to diversion by saying it was not a proposal at all, that in fact it was a statement of objective. But the fact is that we have had from the Prime Minister for the first time, in the limited context in which he used it, a mention of the phrase "British free trade proposal". I think this afternoon was the first time he has even mentioned the phrase in this house.
In spite of repeated questions directed to him-and the Prime Minister will recall that I put some of them to him myself last fall- it has not been possible to get from the right hon. gentleman any reaction whatsoever regarding what the government as a whole thinks about this proposal. And not only are we denied this opportunity in the house, but the Prime Minister apparently took the opportunity, when he was with the British prime minister, of precluding the latter from amplifying details which we on this side of the house have been trying to get from this administration for many months both before and after the election. And if we have not been able to succeed, should those who represent the agencies of communication of this country be denied the opportunity of conveying to the people of Canada the views of the British government in respect of a matter which they regard as so important not only for the United Kingdom but for Canada and


which in the light of the need for interdependence, as the British prime minister said, could mean so much to the world at large in these difficult days of international tension.
I am sure the Prime Minister has not succeeded this afternoon in satisfying this house that he did not by his manner and speech preclude the British prime minister from making a comment in answer to a question submitted to him by the C.B.C., a question which is of the greatest interest to this house and to this country. That is an unwarranted interference with one of the agencies of communication in Canada which it is our duty, just as it was the Prime Minister's duty when he was in opposition and thought there was interference on another occasion, to bring to the attention of the house.
The Prime Minister said in answer to the Leader of the Opposition that he meant what he is reported to have said last year at page 2830 of Hansard, and repeated today. Of course, the Prime Minister is a master in the art of diversion. I do not mean trade diversion; I mean in the art of diversion in debate and in the debate last year he undertook to give a full answer to the comparable though justified allegations made today by the Leader of the Opposition.
Assuming, for argument sake, that the course taken by the Minister of Finance and by the Prime Minister last year with regard to the letter by the former prime minister was valid. That does not in any circumstance justify the action which the Prime Minister took on Friday last. I say: if that course was right a year ago-and I am not saying that it was; I say it was not-that was no reason for the Prime Minister doing what he did on Friday last. As a matter of fact and again assuming for purpose of argument- and I will come to that point later-that there was validity in the position taken last year by the right hon. gentleman and those of his colleagues who sit with him now, compare the difference in the situation; in the one case it was a letter directed in terms apparent for everyone to see and understand-

speechtext: And unproduced.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman, apparently, saw it.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Have you got it?

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM

He apparently saw it, because he told us all about its terms. It was a letter directed to the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the former prime minister denied that it involved the kind of intervention about which the right hon. gentleman complains. But compare that situation with the situation of

last Friday. Here are the British prime minister and the Prime Minister of Canada. Who seeks to put the question? Is it the president of the C.B.C. or the general manager? No. It is a reporter of ordinary status though, I suspect, of great ability. He obviously would be awed by an intervention by the Prime Minister of Canada.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that a comparison of these two situations puts the Prime Minister exactly in the position-only with more reasons attached to him in which he sought to put the former prime minister and whatever the hon. gentleman may say about the incident of last year the fact is there was a denial by the prime minister of that day that he had in any way interfered with the operations of the C.B.C. What is more, any one who knows the character of that right hon. gentleman who formerly sat in the treasury benches knows that any denial made by him is one that would be accepted by any hon. member of this house.
The Prime Minister, again resorted to the capacity he has for diversion and of introducing a red herring-a talent which I as a fellow lawyer certainly cannot help but admire-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: You are good at it yourself.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERFERENCE IN INTERVIEW WITH PRIME MINISTER OF UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for that compliment. The fact is, however, that the Prime Minister on this occasion resorted to another red herring. He introduced the Ostry matter. That, too, was denied. There is no evidence-and I challenge the Prime Minister now to produce it-to support his contention that there was any interference. The only evidence he could produce is a statement by the then minister of national revenue who reported on matters having to do with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that the C.B.C. had advised him in an answer which they prepared and which he presented in this house for reasons of nonadaptability they had cancelled the program. The Prime Minister did not refer to that and so, when he introduces the Ostry matter, he introduces a matter which like the previous one is not in fact a precedent at all and in no way helps to justify the course which the Prime Minister used when he appeared with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom last Friday during the television interview regarding questions being put by the representative of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
By introducing this technique of red herring the Prime Minister said there was no interference in the discussion of these matters. "Why, the president of the Canadian institute of international affairs spoke about this matter on Sunday," said the Prime Minister.
Television Interview-Alleged Interference No one has suggested that this interference by the Prime Minister extends to all programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We realize there are limitations in the mobility of the Prime Minister; there are circumstances beyond the physical control of any man. I heard that broadcast by Professor Mclnnis and I do not recall him saying anything about the British free trade proposal but in any event if he did that does not justify the Prime Minister in precluding a representative of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation from asking a question on the very same subject of the British prime minister.
As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister introduced a fourth red herring this afternoon. He mentioned an important incident involving the nations of the world in the matter of Suez. He forgets that that particular incident recalls the very technique which he apparently used on Friday last. I well recall reading in the paper that after the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) had been sworn in he was asked by the newspaper men of this country what he thought about Canada's foreign policy and what he thought about Suez. The Secretary of States for External Affairs replied and said that he agreed fully with the policy of the present Leader of the Opposition, the former secretary of state for external affairs. At that very point my right hon. and genial friend the Prime Minister said, "No, no, no. The policy of this government is exactly as stated by me in parliament." This left the clear implication that anything said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that is contrary to anything the Prime Minister has ever said must not be uttered and must not be communicated to the press and not even reported by the press. The views of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on important matters of that kind apparently must not run counter to what my right hon. friend as leader of the Conservative party and Prime Minister of Canada thinks and says. And so the technique of "No, no, no" used on Friday last was on one occasion used on the steps of the building that houses the Supreme Court of Canada after the distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs had been sworn in as a member of Her Majesty's privy council.
We all realize that the Prime Minister has heavy responsibilities, that he is a busy man. We can very well understand that there are occasions when his over-all consuming interest in the problems of the nation and of the world are such that he might do things which as the private hon. member for Prince Albert he certainly would not do and which he certainly has alleged should

Television Interview-Alleged Interference not be done. But it is our duty-and I am sure the Prime Minister recognizes it is our duty-to remind him of these excursions into the realm of violation of the kind of freedom which we cherish in this country and which I know he along with every other hon. member of this house would want to see us perpetuate.
The hon. gentleman would do well to remember his own words which the Leader of the Opposition quoted. But if the words quoted by the Leader of the Opposition are effective and bear repetition so, too, do the words of the distinguished Minister of Finance who sits with him. Here is what the Minister of Finance said on March 29, 1957, as recorded at page 2824 of volume 3 of Hansard:
As long as I am a member of parliament I certainly intend to defend Mr. Dunton's right to support the policies and defend the programming activities of the corporation even when I disagree with them. But when there is disagreement, sir, let it be in the proper place, let it be in the houses of parliament. Parliament is supreme; parliament is the body to which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is responsible. And in this particular if, as appears from the statement made by the Prime Minister yesterday, Mr. Dunton resisted the attempt of the Prime Minister to influence the programming activities of the C.B.C., then I say-
And I ask the present Prime Minister to pay special attention to these words:
-then I say this parliament owes a debt of gratitude to Mr. Dunton for having stood firmly for a principle that the Prime Minister ought to have been the first to uphold and which at that time he evidently was discarding and repudiating.
The Prime Minister might well recall other words of his when at the conclusion of his remarks last year as recorded at page 2831 of Hansard he said:
I say to the Prime Minister,-
This is the present Prime Minister speaking-
-and I do not wish to carry the matter any further, but I hope this will be a lesson to the members of this government that interference, indirectly or directly, direct or subtle,-
"No, no, no" might be subtle.
-will not be condoned. Interference of this kind can only destroy the independence of the C.B.C. and dry up the wells of information to which the Canadian people are entitled.
As I have said, we all appreciate that the Prime Minister has heavy responsibilities. They may have been responsible for the statement he made in this house about the press interview given by the secretary general of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization which remarks, incidentally, Mr. Spaak repeated in Halifax after he left Ottawa. We can understand the Prime Minister's concern about the remarks he made about trade diversion with the United Kingdom. We now have

this further incident when the prime minister of the United Kingdom was precluded in his presence from saying to a representative of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation what he thought about a proposal to which this government obviously has not yet given the full and final consideration this question is entitled to receive. I say to the Prime Minister, then, in his own words, "Let this particular occasion be a reminder of the undesirability of this kind of action, and let it not happen again, and let it now be remembered as a result of this debate."
I say to the Prime Minister, too, why does he not take the country into his confidence and tell us what the British prime minister wanted to say about the proposal? It certainly deserves at least from this government a statement that it is prepared to give this question of British free trade the kind of sympathetic attention that one would expect this government to give to a friendly government like Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom. That, surely, is not asking too much of the Prime Minister and we all trust he will not make this mistake again.

ALLEGED DIS- CRIMINATION IN PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we got very far with the last grievance but I hope we can get a little farther with this one. It is a matter involving some hundreds of people in the city of Vancouver, including a considerable number in my own constituency of Vancouver East. I have always found it very difficult to understand why the government has not seen fit to alter the federal regulations pertaining
[Mr. Pickersgill.)
to eligibility for unemployment insurance whereby they now deny the opportunity and right to people drawing unemployment insurance benefits to try to obtain employment in the longshoring trade even if only for a few hours. I do not know the reasons for the regulation because to the best of my knowledge it applies only to the longshoring trade.
If a person is eligible for unemployment insurance benefits and in order to help himself gets a few hours work in any other trade and earns a few dollars, he does not become ineligible to continue drawing his unemployment insurance benefits, but if he gets even as little as two and a half hours work as a longshoreman he is immediately denied the right to draw unemployment insurance in the two week period that is involved. To me this is a most iniquitous regulation. I could give a great number of examples but I will refer only to one in order to prove my contention.
This case came to my attention recently. It concerns one of my constituents who by occupation is a logger. He has been unemployed and has been drawing unemployment insurance since December 14, 1957. Recently he decided he would try to get employment somewhere and he sought work as a longshoreman. To get work as a longshoreman you have to obtain what is known as a stevedore's registration number. He did so and he worked for two and a half hours on Tuesday, May 27. He earned $6.50. On the following day, which happened to be the day for payment of his unemployment insurance benefit, he received his unemployment insurance cheque for $30. He made out a statutory declaration as required by law advising the unemployment insurance commission office in Vancouver that he had worked two and a half hours as a longshoreman and had earned $6.50. He was immediately told that because he had worked two and a half hours as a longshoreman he was not eligible to draw his $30 and would have to wait for two weeks until the payroll statement of the company employing the longshoremen had been checked.
He was denied payment although he had only worked two and a half hours as a longshoreman. This man is married and has two children, a young girl of seven and a half and a boy two years and three months old. There was no food at all for the family and he was not eligible for any other assistance. It was just by the grace of God that we were able to have the Salvation Army provide him with temporary relief.
When the case was appealed to the unemployment insurance commission in Vancouver the officials were most co-operative and helpful but they said there was nothing they could do about it because of the regulation

of the commission in Ottawa and that they had to abide by it. Here is a rather amazing situation. The chief claims agent-I forget his exact title but I think that is correct- in the unemployment insurance office in Vancouver told this man that if he would give up his stevedoring registration number he could immediately pay him his unemployment insurance. This man was trying to obtain a little bit of work in order to get some money to help his family but because he did so in the longshoring field and although he only worked for two and a half hours his endeavours to become a useful and productive member of society were curtailed and hampered. The only way he can draw his unemployment insurance benefits is by giving up his stevedoring permit number.
As I said, the employees in the office in Vancouver were most co-operative and helpful but they said they could not do anything about it because of the Ottawa regulations. I have only cited one case but I could refer the minister to hundreds of a similar nature. This is an absolutely vicious and iniquitous practice. It is a vicious, iniquitous regulation. I felt that I should draw this grievance to the attention of the government because it should be correced immediately.
The matter probably comes under the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) but unfortunately he has been away for a great many days. However, I note the evident interest of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) who also comes from Vancouver and who knows something about the longshoring trade and the unemployment situation there. If he cannot give the matter personal consideration I trust that he will see that it is drawn to the attention of the proper officials to see if the situation cannot be corrected.
Although I am not going to go into details at the moment I hope the government will also look into the situation in the city of Vancouver as far as the payment of unemployment insurance benefits to longshoremen is concerned. To the best of my knowledge they are the only group who in respect of unemployment insurance are classified as second class Canadians in that different regulations apply to them from those that apply to people engaged in any other occupation, regulations of such a nature that these men pay more and receive less when it comes to benefits.
I know that in the past a brief was presented to the government and I was informed only this morning that a new brief is being prepared for presentation. I am not going into this matter at the moment except to draw it to the attention of the government.
In so far as this other matter is concerned, this major grievance where a casual worker
Pipe Lines-Labour Conditions for only 2J hours was cut off unemployment insurance, I hope for speedy action by the government.

Mr. Speaker, in so far as this question of unemployment insurance is concerned, I should like to bring to the attention of the house a problem concerning young people who, being entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, try to use their spare time by attending local schools and are denied the right to draw their unemployment insurance benefits. There is something rather unfair about this particular regulation.
I have a number of people in my riding who during the summer engaged in the fishing industry and were thereby well qualified for unemployment insurance benefits during the winter. Employment was extremely difficult to get, and rather than spend the time doing nothing they decided to go back to school. The moment they entered the school their unemployment insurance benefits were cut off. In my opinion there is something wrong when a young lad qualifies himself for unemployment insurance benefits, and then is denied those benefits because he tries to use his spare time profitably.
If I may put it another way, it seems to me there is something wrong with a scheme of this kind which pays a young man to waste his time. I would say again that this is one problem which certainly needs some investigation. It is a question that needs very careful attention. At the moment, it does appear that these regulations governing unemployment insurance are a little too rigid in many cases and need the attention of the unemployment insurance commission.

I should like to raise another matter which appears day by day to become more important in this country. I am referring to the situation with regard to natural gas, and all its aspects across this country. No useful purpose will be served by going into past history, with which most of us are familiar. Certainly, the history should be familiar to the government because this matter had a great deal to do with the fact the government is sitting on that side of the house today. There are many references on the record also concerning the change of heart the government has had since they left this side of the house concerning the trans-Canada pipe line issue.
I should like to deal in more detail with what might be called some of the side issues that have been raised with regard to this great Canadian utility. It appears to me

Pipe Lines-Labour Conditions that this whole issue of natural gas, trans-Canada pipe lines and the distributing lines, is nothing more nor less than an evil tree which, with all its evil branches, seems to be spreading across this country. Conceived in the rape of our natural resources by people who were referred to by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) as those Texas buccaneers, this evil tree has grown in the west and has spread towards the east, with every one of its branches appearing to be just as troublesome and just as evil as the tree itself. We have seen nothing but labour problems all the way across the country, starting with the infamous back-door agreement which was signed with a hit-and-run union before the employees were hired. They were forced into a union which they had never seen, the stewards of which they had never seen and which could not properly serve their interests. This master contract was signed in Alberta and covered all future employees.
We have seen some of the results of this action. There was the big strike at the head of the lakes around the Hearst area which tied up the whole operation for a period of three weeks last winter. The federal Department of Labour had to step in on that occasion in an effort to settle the matter so that the company could proceed with clearing the right of way and laying the pipe. The troubles did not end there. In fact, they were just getting nicely started. On two different occasions during the month of March I had to appeal to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) because clauses of this agreement, signed under the supervision of and with the assistance of the Department of Labour, were being violated. I should like to compliment the minister at this stage upon the speed with which he acted to correct the situation. On one particular occasion I sent a telegram to the minister's office one afternoon, and the following morning I received a telephone call from one of the top officials of Trans-Canada.

When the house adjourned at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with some of the labour problems which have arisen with respect to the trans-Canada pipe line, particularly in northern Ontario. In all fairness, and in spite of the record across the country, I would like to say that a lot of the trouble has not been the fault of the pipe line company-that is to say the parent company-but has been the fault

of some of the contractors, subcontractors and sub-subcontractors. It appears that quite a spider's web of subcontracting is going on up there, and how things can be split so many times with everybody showing a profit is something which I cannot understand or explain to this house. However, it does involve difficulties when one tries to iron out any of these grievances; it is something like being in the middle of a northern swamp in the month of June when the mosquitoes are at their worst, not knowing just which mosquito is doing the biting.
Another convenient arrangement, and this of course applies to the period after the base rate was established following the strike in January, when there was an increase of a matter of 20 cents per hour to bring the base rate fairly close to the local rate, is where we get a group of employees, many of whom unfortunately may not be too well educated, being told "the rate here is $1.40 per hour but you don't want to work for as low a rate as that, you should do it on a piecework basis." After a good sales job they are convinced they can make themselves a fortune in a very short time, so they go in on a contract basis but find at the end of three or four weeks that all they are making is about 90 cents an hour instead of $1.40.
We have received many other complaints about how part of their pay has been held back for various reasons and now there is apparently a brand new gimmick altogether. In place of hiring local men who by this time are quite familiar with the agreement signed following the strike, they seem to be giving preference to people from outside the province and, indeed, in many cases from outside the country altogether. Such new men are not familiar with the agreement covering the projects and they make certain that these men do not stay on the job long enough to become familiar with it. After a few days' work they are laid off and others hired in their places. As recently as June 4 last I received a communication listing some of the problems I have raised and asking advice as to what could be done about them.
Another aspect of the matter which has affected this project right across the country has to do with the rights of way across farm properties. I am reminded, Mr. Speaker, of nothing so much as a wolf pack after the moose in winter; they pick off the moose one by one. Every known device in the selling field is used to have these men sign agreements, often without reading the small print and so on and so forth. The majority of them perhaps feel they could not afford legal advice to interpret the fine print in any event. As a result, they are picked off one by one. It might be wise to give a word of advice to

the farmers who will become affected from now on. I might suggest that they might take an example from the moose and that if they, like the moose, keep together they will find they can protect themselves against the wolf pack.
This leads me to another aspect, probably the most important aspect of this whole question; that is the newspaper headlines which follow this project across Canada. I am speaking particularly of the scandal associated with municipal and provincial authorities right up to cabinet rank. We have seen some evidence of this in the province of Ontario and I believe there are one or two investigations going on in regard to this matter at the present time. The most significant thing about it is that while there are relatively few men who have abused the privileges and trust placed in them by the electorate, the fact nevertheless remains that the innocent are smeared along with the guilty, and it has now reached the stage where it is quite conceivable that the respect and trust in elected officials across Canada will be severely shaken. We have seen what has happened in the province of Ontario and, in the last few days, we have seen that this malignant tree has spread its roots into the province of Quebec-

Pipe Lines-Labour Conditions clauses granting privileges to the private companies building the lines, including the right of expropriation. They were granted the right to use a farmer's land with or without his agreement, but in my opinion adequate provision was never made for the rights and interests of those who were forced to give up their land. In my own riding of Timiskaming, when the officials of the company applied for easements they went to the farmers and said: this is only an option, we would like to pay you $5; we would also like to buy four acres of your 160-acre farm, having in mind the fact that the land required was only 66 feet wide and the rest was a linear measurement. At the same time they implied that whatever the farmer might decide; the federal government had already given them the right of expropriation.
I have looked into this question of expropriation to some extent, and I find that the company has been given that right. I have also found that very little protection has been given to the farmer who is faced with expropriation. In this case, although the farmers were inclined to stick together and deal collectively with the officials the pipe line company said they could not do this and that they had no intention of dealing with the farmers in this way. They played one farmer off against another. I think that having given the pipe line company the right to apply for expropriation, the right to easements, we should have given the farmers some protection by setting up an impartial board which would evaluate farm land.
I should like to call attention to a case which happened a few weeks ago in the riding of Timiskaming where a young couple, a veteran and his wife had applied to the Department of Veterans Affairs for money with which to start a tourist camp to be installed on a nice piece of land near a very suitable lake. They had applied to the department and were waiting to hear whether they could get money to start this motel. In the meantime the pipe line company came along with a crew on a Sunday night when people were not normally on that property, cut down the trees, brought in their bulldozers and cleared a stretch 60 feet wide. When the people concerned complained to the officials-the provincial police and other authorities-they were told that there was no redress and that if they wished to start an action for trespass they would have to go to proper legal channels. In this particular case the people had asked the Department of Veterans Affairs to send an evaluator and this official had set a valuation on this property in accordance with the plans which had been prepared 
for its development many months before, and his valuation of the land, and of the detrimental effect that this pipe line would have on it, was three times what the owners of the property were offered by the company.
I think that when we gave the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited the right to construct this public utility we should have given greater protection to those with whom the company has to deal. It is all very well to tell a farmer that he can take the company to court, but it is my understanding that in the riding of Timiskaming there is not one lawyer who is willing to conduct such cases against the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. I know for a fact that the attorney general's department is not too willing to press trespass charges against the company, because I have made inquiries and have been informed that they are not willing to do so. The farmers in my part of the country are not sufficiently well off to spend thousands of dollars fighting against something they did not ask for in the first place.
The government of Canada has the responsibility for protecting these people. While I agree that we must allow this public utility to expropriate the land required we must also see to it that the people who are affected receive an adequate amount of money in return. It was accepted by some of the farmers at their meetings that they would be quite happy to settle for a basic sum of $50 an acre. They pointed out that if the company had to pay $200 to clear the land, then if the land had already been cleared, surely it would be worth at least that amount; the amount it would have cost, in any case, to clear. I believe the payment of $50 plus $200, making a total payment of $250, is a fair and reasonable price.
The contract set out certain things that would be done on behalf of a man who sold property. They undertook to close in the trenches and do clean-up work. They went so far as to state that they would seed the ground, grade it and place grass on it thereby making it very nice for the farmer. I understand that has not been done in most cases in western Ontario where the pipe line passed through. I do not think it will be done in Timiskaming because the people agreed to an over-all sum which would include damages and signed away or waived all rights to court procedure with respect to damage. I believe we have an obligation to look at the matter not only for the present pipeline but in order to set a precedent for the future. There is a popular rumour to the effect that it will not be long until a second and third line are put in.

Another problem with which it is difficult to deal is that of labour. We have no objection to United States companies and it is true that many have a large investment, perhaps $3 million worth of equipment. While it is true they should be allowed to bring in from the United States their overseers, foremen and employees above that rank I do not think it is necessary or desirable to allow them to bring in shovel operators, backline operators and workers of that type. In Ontario we have many competent shovel operators and other workers with many years of experience on construction crews. They would be perfectly capable of doing the work and this would obviate the necessity of bringing in men from other countries.
There has been a question raised as to whether this is a matter of federal concern. Certainly the question of bringing in United States workers to work on Canadian pipe lines comes under federal jurisdiction. We are faced with an odd situation when we cannot find out from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration how many United States workers were employed on a particular spread. In the contract governing the employment of workers for the section of the pipe line that is operated by the crown corporation all United States workers must be hired only with the consent of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) but the bulk of the people who have been brought in to work on the pipe line are from the United States. I must admit that we in Timiskaming refer to them as "you-all's". I suppose that is because many of them come from Texas and speak with a southern drawl: "How are you all?" These people do not enter Canada under a work permit. They come as landed immigrants and have no citizenship papers. They can move freely from place to place and stay as long as they wish. When a job is finished they can return to the United States to pursue their occupation elsewhere.
It is interesting to note how those charged with the responsibility of hiring employees to work on the pipe line avoid the use of the unemployment insurance offices. I believe that people seeking employment on construction jobs should not be required to line up in front of a construction shack at six o'clock in the morning while the boss comes out, strolls up and down, and says, "You and you and you work today; the rest of you be back here at six o'clock tomorrow morning." I can remember occasions like that when I went to work in the mines of northern Ontario at the end of the thirties and the beginning of the forties. Management thought it was wonderful to have 300 men lined up at the gate seeking to fill two vacancies. I thought those days had passed for all time.
Pipe Lines-Labour Conditions
One of the failings of the unemployment insurance commission is that it cannot guarantee that a man sent to a job as a shovel operator, for instance, is fully qualified in his occupation. We have no system in Canada under which we can determine who is and who is not qualified for a particular job. It frequently happens that a man sent to a job who has five or six years experience in his occupation is told by management at the end of half an hour that he is not qualified to do the work or has insufficient experience and someone is brought in to replace him who might have been employed by the company on a previous occasion, perhaps in western Canada. The unions are unable to do much in this regard because they are not in close contact with the situation. In most cases they have hiring clauses in their contracts but they are not in a position to say that a man is qualified for a particular assignment and when a company says he is not qualified that is usually the end of the matter.
It has been said there are not sufficient trained welders in Canada, and that this accounts for their working double shifts. If we have not a sufficient number of qualified welders in Canada I say it is a disgrace to the people of this country that we should not be capable of suitably training people to do this type of work.
I would like to discuss the common labourer for a moment. Surely no one would contend we have an insufficient number of these men or that they are required to work double shifts. Many of these men who earn $1.25 an hour are working 70 or more hours each week. In view of the serious unemployment situation that exists in northern Ontario we should be able to enforce a 40-hour week for common labourers and thus employ two people on a job where we are now employing only one. This would not mean delaying the pipe-line contractors. Indeed this would be undesirable as they have a short season and must accomplish as much as possible during good weather. However, a swing shift system would offer employment to many people who are seeking it and each common labourer could do a reasonable amount of work and we could perhaps employ two or three men where we are now employing only one.
The matter of working on Sunday has become a great problem deserving the attention of the federal government. We have piously enacted the Lord's Day Act which sets out that no work should be done on Sunday if the operation is not continuous but we do not see fit to enforce the provisions of this legislation. I am pleased to state, however, that the townspeople in my area have taken matters into their own hands. They went out

Pipe Lines-Labour Conditions on Sundays when they did not have very much to do themselves and made such a fuss about it with the contractors that the contractors have now shut down except for maintenance work on Sundays.
These are questions we as Canadians are going to have to face. If transmission lines are to be built across Canada then we should have regulations to protect the Canadian people. My colleague, the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) mentioned the fact that this line would have been more satisfactorily handled if it had been entirely done through a crown corporation. I believe this truth will be borne out in time based on the success we had in putting through the line in the northern Ontario section which is now owned jointly by the federal and provincial governments. The work progressed very rapidly and the Department of Defence Production has done an exceptionally good job in this field. The problem of stock distribution could have been prevented if we had seen fit to make the entire pipe line a public utility.
I would urge the federal government to give full consideration at least to this matter of controlling the price, setting up the board of transport commissioners to control the price of gas coming through northern Ontario. As everybody knows, northern Ontario has now progressed past the original state of development where it depended on and could live off its natural resources. We are now sorely in need of secondary industries. While in the town of Timmins a unit of gas is quoted at $2.40, yet in the city of Cornwall, which will be another 500 miles along the line, that same unit of gas is being quoted at $1.40. The board of transport commissioners could do a great service to the people of northern Ontario by making gas as readily and as cheaply available as possible to encourage the introduction of new industries. I urge that some control be exercised over pipe lines in general and the trans Canada pipe line in particular, and that before we grant a licence to another pipe-line company to build a line across Canada we insist on some protection for the workers and the farmers who will be directly affected by the line.
I would point out that this is not a radical change for the Conservative government because only a year or so ago while in opposition the members of the Conservative party were pleased to support a different policy on natural gas. I would strongly urge that they consider now the implementation of that policy.

I wonder whether the minister has had an opportunity to look at the specifications regarding the two buildings now being constructed in St. John's? Perhaps the minister can do that at some later date; I know he cannot do it at once. If he would do that I would personally like to see how those specificatons are worded because, even though there may be an escape clause which would permit other products to be used, if one product is specifically mentioned it can be interpreted by the contractor as being the first choice, and any other substitutions would perhaps be regarded as to be used only if the former were not available.
This is a very important point as far as Newfoundland is concerned, and I do hope the minister will be able to give us all the information possible on this point. Before I sit down I would like to bring to the attention of the minister and through him to his colleagues in the government-because this will

concern the cabinet as a whole-a situation which has developed in Newfoundland due to the difference in policies in regard to public buildings before and since Newfoundland joined confederation. Before Newfoundland became a province of Canada the construction of public buildings was the responsibility of the provincial government, and they had a very simple policy which was based mainly on the size of the community, and also on the fact that in Newfoundland we had a special situation with respect to post offices and telegraph offices. These two services were combined into a single service prior to Newfoundland becoming a province of Canada and as it was not suitable for those services to be performed in private homes the provincial government built a public building in the community for those services.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
That was
not so everywhere.

My hon. friend can tell his story after I have finished; I am going to tell mine. After Newfoundland became a province of Canada, the maintenance and the construction of public buildings became the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government has a different policy altogether. For example, post offices are built only in communities where the revenue from the sale of stamps is around $10,000. You have to have a very large fishing community to have stamp sales of that magnitude.
The situation which I wish to bring to the minister's attention is this. In a community of about 200 or 300 families before confederation that community would have a public building of its own, a small public building for the post office department and for the telegraph office.

Can you
name some of them?

Yes, Bay L'Argent, is one; Burgeo is another; Gaultois is a third in my riding. I could name dozens of those places. The point I want to make is that where those buildings had to be replaced they have been replaced by the federal government and have been improved upon. If my hon. friend wants an example I can give him a beautiful example which the minister himself mentioned, namely Harbour Buffett. Harbour Buffett is an example of a public building in a small community of about 500 people. The time came when that building had to be replaced, rebuilt, and now, as the minister pointed out last Friday, a very nice public building is being erected in Harbour Buffett, which is far better and a great credit to the minister, to his department and also to the federal
Supply-Public Works government which provided the funds for it prior to the general election of June 10.
We have in this community a very fine public building but the point is that in my own riding and in Newfoundland generally there are many other communities of the same size that did not happen to have public buildings prior to confederation and under the present policy of the federal government these communities cannot get a separate public building. I hope the minister will look into that situation to see what can be done so that we may have a uniform policy in Newfoundland with respect to public buildings.

Then when the contract was let and the work commenced, it was found that there was water trouble in the excavation, and that has been the reason for the delay. There has been a great deal of difficulty in connection with water. I happened to visit Newcastle-
I am aware of that, during the campaign.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

I hope the hon. member felt my presence. I had the pleasure of visiting Newcastle during the election campaign and I noticed that the building was not getting ahead as I had hoped it would. Mr. Chairman, I sort of expected the answer the minister was going to give me and that is why I prefaced my remarks by certain quotations which appear in Hansard. With regard to the building in Quebec city, this has caused great concern because we are particularly anxious to get ahead with this building. As the hon. member for Levis knows, the Department of Public Works has a site but the planning commission of the city of Quebec would not let us build a federal building on that site. Shortly after I became minister I wrote to the mayor of Quebec asking for an early decision on this aspect of the question.
Could the minister give me the date of that letter?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have not the date here but it was some time last fall and I pointed out our desire to get on with the building as quickly as possible and then, on December 30, the mayor replied requesting a meeting. We met with him in Ottawa on January 27 and it appeared during that discussion that a stalemate had been reached in the negotiations between the railway and the city with respect to the exchange of land. The city wanted to have this federal building on a site owned by Canadian National Railways and we suggested that the federal government should bypass the C.N.R. property and exchange our site for a property further to the east which could be acquired by the city without involving either the Canadian National Railways station or the track. This suggestion seemed to find favour with the city officials as did our suggestion that any exchange of properties would be on a value for value basis. On February 25 we repeated these proposals and again expressed the need for early action. On March 16 the mayor advised us that no decision was possible before April and, to date, we have had no further word from the mayor of Quebec.
We have, however, had a verbal communication to the effect that the Canadian National Railways was prepared to demolish its station and to make the land available


for construction of a federal building provided the city would agree that buses could be substituted on the Quebec city-Ste. Anne de Beaupre run. My understanding is that the city of Quebec also has this information but we do not know what progress has been made with respect to reaching an agreement with Canadian National Railways. That is the way the matter stands at the moment. We are only too glad to do everything we can to facilitate the construction of the building, but we cannot force the Canadian National Railways to demolish its station and give up the land.

Would the minister tell me whether the Canadian National Railways is still asking the same price for the site where the old station is located? I have a distinct recollection that they were asking about $540,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The department has never been given information concerning the amount the Canadian National Railways was asking for the site. It is between the city and the Canadian National Railways.

I think the minister will find the information on the file, if I remember correctly. I did, of course, take a special interest in this matter because it is near my home town and I do remember that the figure was $540,000. In any event, I would ask the minister if he would take some steps to try to get the C.N.R. and the city together. He could also obtain the help of the Minister of Transport, which I think was the policy followed by the previous government, in endeavouring to get the two parties to reach an agreement. My fear is that otherwise a generation will pass without the city of Quebec having its federal post office built.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We cannot force the hand of the Canadian National Railways and, incidentally, we could build the building on the site on the other side of the station if the city officials were agreeable.

I know that the minister cannot force the C.N.R. but he does know from past experience that we are paying deficits for the C.N.R. and certainly with the help of the Minister of Transport I think he could do a lot to get the two parties together. Even the Prime Minister could assist in this regard as did the previous prime minister. In this connection I know that the former prime minister in the last few months of his administration took steps to even see the president of the Canadian National Railways. The minister is well aware, as is also the Postmaster General, that this building

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask leave to revert to motions in order to move that the estimates of the Department of Transport be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As I explained on an earlier occasion, Mr. Speaker, when we were considering an amendment to the standing orders to set up a standing committee on veterans affairs and one on estimates for this year, we planned to try out referring certain of the estimates to standing committees and I instanced the referring of estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to the committee on lands, forests and waters and the estimates of the Department of Fisheries to the standing committee on marine and fisheries; the estimates of the Department of Labour to the standing committee on industrial relations and I think I also referred to the Department of Transport estimates and suggested they would be referred to this standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. In addition, of course, the estimates of the Department of External Affairs are to be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
We are trying, in addition to having those particular estimates referred to these standing committees which I have mentioned, to have the estimates committee review several of the departments' estimates and they are now working on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. I expect one of these days they will request that the estimates of certain other departments be referred to them but we do have to keep some estimates for consideration in the house. Until tonight we only had public works and agriculture which could be considered in this committee of supply but we now also have the estimates of trade and commerce and of justice which were put in tonight.
It so happens that there is a standing committee which we think could very well deal with the estimates of the Department of Transport and we propose to try out this plan. If it does not work out satisfactorily then

I refer to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and, as the hon. member for Laurier knows, this has been one of the best committees of the house. He and I have always served on it and I am sure he will find this plan will be fairly successful.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not complaining about the plan but I thank the house leader for the explanation he has given to this house. On the contrary, I would think, as the Leader of the Opposition has already stated, that in so far as the three departments which were referred to by the house leader are concerned, namely national defence, northern affairs and veterans affairs, there would be no objection from this side of the house to their being referred to their respective committees, but there has been no agreement with respect to the Department of Transport. I am taking no position at this moment other than to say it seems to me that the Deparment of Transport, being such an important and large department-as is the minister's own department-its estimates should be considered by the whole house rather than by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. That is a committee, to my way of thinking, which is charged with a certain responsibility and it would seem to me that it is not the committee to which the estimates of this department should go. My suggestion would be, if my hon. friend would agree, that he might allow this motion to stand until tomorrow so that I may discuss it with the Leader of the Opposition after which we could come to some agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have no objection to that but I would point out to the hon. member for Laurier that if the course we suggest is followed the transport estimates will be considered twice, first of all in the standing committee and then in committee of the whole house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: We will be perfectly satisfied if they are considered but once.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Probably they would not be brought on for consideration in the house for some considerable time if they did not go to the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: If the motion stands, we will leave the matter there.

speechtext:
What amount was paid to (a) the province of Quebec; (b) the province of Ontario, under the Tax Rental Agreements Act (i) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957; (ii) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958?
Answer by: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
1956-	57, the Tax Rental Agreements Act, 1952: Quebec, nil; Ontario, $160,558,129.
1957-	58, the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act: Quebec, equalization payment only, $43,060,000; Ontario, tax rental payment for individual income tax only, $74,379,000.
These payments do not include the share of income tax of certain public utility corporations. Under section 6 of the Tax Rental Agreements Act, 1952, all provinces are entitled to 50 per cent of such payment of federal income tax.
1956-	57: Quebec, $1,186,280; Ontario, $1,428,408.
1957-	58: Quebec, $1,675,230; Ontario, $1,333,166.
